questions.q: Your Task API saves its tasks to a JSON file. Which problem does the lesson say this causes?
questions.explain: A file has no protection for many writers at once and no way to undo a half-finished write. A database is built exactly for these jobs: safe concurrent writes, crash recovery and fast lookups.
options: Two requests writing at the same moment can overwrite each other, and a crash mid-write can leave a broken file
Node.js can only read a JSON file once
JSON files are always slower to read than a network call

questions.q: Which database family stores a value under a key, like a giant Map?
questions.explain: Key-value stores such as Redis and Valkey look up a value by its key. Relational databases store tables of rows and columns; document databases store JSON-like documents.

questions.q: Why does the lesson call relational (SQL) databases the right default for most backends?
questions.explain: A relational database enforces column types, required values and links between tables. Everything that is not relational is often called NoSQL.
options: They are the only databases that can store text
They check the shape of your data and link records safely
They do not need any schema

questions.q: What is PGlite?
questions.explain: PGlite needs no separate server and no password, which makes it perfect for learning and for tests. The next lesson installs a normal PostgreSQL server.
options: A smaller SQL language that only looks like PostgreSQL
The real PostgreSQL, compiled to WebAssembly so it runs inside your Node.js program
A cloud service that hosts PostgreSQL for free
A JSON file format for storing tables

questions.q: You create a database with new PGlite() and add some rows. What happens to them when the program ends?
questions.explain: Without an argument, PGlite starts an empty database in memory each time. Pass a folder, new PGlite("./data"), to keep it on disk.
options: They are gone: the database lived only in memory
They are saved in the browser's local storage

questions.q: Why does the lesson write db.query("insert into tasks (title) values ($1)", [title]) instead of putting title into the SQL text?
questions.explain: Always pass outside values as parameters. Gluing user input into SQL text allows SQL injection, which the next lesson demonstrates.
options: Placeholders make the query run twice as fast
PostgreSQL does not accept text values inside SQL
The value is sent separately from the SQL text, so outside input can never change the query itself
The array is needed so the database can pick the next id

questions.q: In PGlite, what is the difference between db.exec and db.query as the lesson uses them?
questions.explain: Use exec for fixed SQL such as create table, and query(sql, params) whenever a statement includes values, especially values from outside.
options: exec runs one or more statements (used for setup); query runs one statement with placeholder values
exec is for PostgreSQL; query is for MySQL
They are the same function with two names

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The database picks the ids 1, 2, … by itself, and the column default fills in done as false. rows is an array of plain objects.

questions.q: Which two rules does a primary key enforce?
questions.explain: A primary key identifies each row, so it is unique and not null. It can be a number (id) or a natural key from the data, like a tag's name.
options: It must be a number, and it must be the first column
No two rows may share it, and it can never be empty
It must be text, and it must be unique per user
It must be sorted, and it can change at any time

questions.q: Why let the database pick ids with generated always as identity instead of computing "highest id + 1" in your code?
questions.explain: Two requests could both read "highest id is 7" and both pick 8. The database hands out the numbers itself, so they never collide.
options: Two requests at the same moment could compute the same id; the database never hands out the same one twice
Identity ids are secret, so users cannot guess them

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The second insert breaks the primary key. PostgreSQL's error code 23505 always means "unique violation". It is a database code, not an HTTP status: your API turns it into 409 Conflict.

questions.q: A sign-up request fails with PostgreSQL error code 23505 on the email column. What should your API answer?
questions.explain: 23505 is a unique violation: the value already exists. That is a conflict with the current state, so 409 fits. Do not forward raw database messages to the client.
options: 409 Conflict, saying the email is already in use

questions.q: email is unique. What does this print?
questions.explain: Text comparison in PostgreSQL is case-sensitive, so the two emails are different values and both rows are saved. Store emails in one form (for example lower case) before you insert them.

questions.q: Each comment is on one task, and a task has many comments. Where does the key go?
questions.explain: One-to-many: put the foreign key on the "many" side. A task cannot hold a single comment_id, because it has many comments.
options: A list of comment ids in a text column on tasks

questions.q: Students take many courses, and each course has many students. How do you store this?
questions.explain: Many-to-many: neither table can hold a single id for the other, so a third table holds one row per link.
options: A join table such as enrollments (student_id, course_id)

questions.q: Each user has at most one settings row. How does the lesson make sure no user gets two?
questions.explain: A unique foreign key turns one-to-many into one-to-one. In the lesson's profiles table, user_id is both the primary key and the foreign key.
options: By checking in JavaScript before every insert
By putting a settings_id on users with no rules
By putting a user_id on settings and making it unique (or the primary key)

questions.q: task_tags has the primary key (task_id, tag_id). What does this print?
questions.explain: The pair must be unique, not each column on its own. Task 1 may have many tags and tag 1 may be on many tasks, but the same tag cannot be added to the same task twice.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: A foreign key must point at a row that exists. User 99 does not exist, so the database refuses the task instead of storing an orphan row forever.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: on delete cascade deletes the user's tasks together with the user. Only user 2's task is left.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: on delete set null keeps the tasks but clears their link to the deleted project. cascade would have deleted task 1 instead.
options: [ { id: 1, project_id: null }, { id: 2, project_id: null } ]

questions.q: What does references users (id) on delete cascade on tasks.user_id mean?
questions.explain: The cascade flows from the referenced row (the user) to the rows that point at it (the tasks). Without any on delete rule, deleting a user who still has tasks is refused.
options: A user cannot be deleted while they have tasks
When a user is deleted, their tasks are deleted too
When a task is deleted, its user is deleted too
Deleted users are copied into the tasks table

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: A title of only spaces trims to length 0, and priority 7 is outside 1 to 3. The database refuses both, whichever program tries the insert, so two rows are saved.

questions.q: The database has check and not null constraints. Should your API still validate input?
questions.explain: The API gives clients clear errors. Constraints protect the data from bugs, scripts run by hand, and a second service that forgot a check.
options: No, the constraints make API validation useless
Yes: the API answers with a friendly 400, and constraints are the last line of defence against bugs and other writers
No, validation in two places is always a bug

questions.q: Which PostgreSQL column type does the lesson name for money?
questions.explain: numeric stores exact decimals, so there is no 0.1 + 0.2 rounding problem. timestamptz is a date and time with time zone.

questions.q: Which columns get an index automatically in PostgreSQL?
questions.explain: Foreign keys like tasks.user_id are exactly what you filter and join by, yet they get no index. Add one yourself.
options: Primary keys and unique columns, but not foreign keys
No columns; you must always create every index yourself

questions.q: No index exists on user_id. What does this print?
questions.explain: Without an index on user_id, the database has to read every one of the 50,000 rows and keep the matches: a sequential scan. The primary key index only helps when you search by id.
options: Index Scan using tasks_pkey on tasks

questions.q: Why not simply add an index to every column?
questions.explain: Every write must update every index on the table. Add indexes for the columns you actually search, filter, join and sort by.
options: PostgreSQL allows only one index per table
Each index takes disk space and makes every insert and update a little slower
Indexes delete rows that are not used often

questions.q: What is an index?
questions.explain: Without an index the database reads every row (a sequential scan), which gets slower as the table grows. An index finds the matches directly.
options: A copy of the whole table kept as a backup
A sorted lookup structure that jumps straight to the matching rows, like the index at the back of a book
The row number of each row
A list of the queries that ran most often

questions.q: Which ACID letter means "all or nothing: if one statement fails, every change in the transaction is undone"?
questions.explain: Atomic: the transaction cannot be split. Isolated means others do not see your half-finished changes; durable means a committed change survives a crash.

questions.q: The database says "committed", and a second later the power goes out. Which ACID promise says the change is still there after restart?
questions.explain: Durable: once committed, the change survives a crash or power cut. Consistent means every constraint still holds when the transaction ends.

questions.q: The second statement breaks a check constraint. What does this print?
questions.explain: Both statements ran in one transaction. When the insert failed, the owner change was rolled back too, so the task still belongs to Ada.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The failed insert used up number 2, and generated numbers are never handed back. Ids can have gaps, so never use them to count rows.

questions.q: Moving a task from Ada to Alan also writes a line to an activity log. Why wrap both statements in a transaction?
questions.explain: The two changes only make sense together. A transaction makes them all happen or none happen. Others do not see the half-finished state (isolation).
options: So the two statements run in parallel and finish faster
So a crash or error between them cannot leave the task moved without a log line, or the other way round
Because update only works inside a transaction
So other clients can see the change before it is finished

questions.q: Tasks need a new due_date column, and production already holds real data. What do you do?
questions.explain: The create table already ran and will not run again, and dropping the table destroys data. A migration is a small change that runs exactly once, in order, on every database.
options: Edit the original create table statement and restart the server
Drop the table and create it again with the new column
Write a new numbered migration, such as alter table tasks add column due_date date
Add the field in JavaScript only, without changing the database
Ask every developer to add the column by hand

questions.q: Migration 3 already ran on production. You notice it should also have created an index. What is the safe fix?
questions.explain: Every database that ran migration 3 has it recorded and will never run it again, so an edit would never reach them. A new id runs everywhere exactly once.
options: Edit migration 3; the runner will notice the change
Add a new migration 4 that creates the index
Delete the row for migration 3 from schema_migrations in production

questions.q: Why does the lesson's runner apply each migration inside a transaction together with its schema_migrations row?
questions.explain: The schema change and the "this ran" record succeed or fail together. After a failure you fix the migration and run it again cleanly.
options: To run all migrations at the same time
A failing migration leaves no half-changed table behind and is not marked as done
So the migration can be edited later
Because alter table is not allowed outside a transaction

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The first run applies both and records their ids. The second run finds both ids in schema_migrations and does nothing, which is exactly what makes it safe to run on every start.

questions.q: A runner decides which migrations still need to run. What does this print?
questions.explain: Only migrations whose ids are not recorded yet will run. Each migration runs exactly once on each database, whatever its position in the list.

questions.q: This JavaScript does what a join through task_tags does. What does it print?
questions.explain: A join produces one row per link, so "Write report" appears twice: once per tag. Three links give three rows.

questions.q: Finish toHttp(error). A PostgreSQL error with code "23505" (unique violation) becomes { status: 409, detail: "Already exists." }. Any other error becomes { status: 500, detail: "Internal error." }. Never copy error.message into the answer.
questions.explain: Branch on the stable code, not on the message text. The raw message names your tables and constraints, so it goes to the server log, not to the client.
questions.expected:
{ status: 409, detail: 'Already exists.' }
{ status: 500, detail: 'Internal error.' }

questions.q: Finish pending(migrations, appliedIds). It returns the names of the migrations that have not run yet, sorted by id (the list may be out of order).
questions.explain: Migrations run in order, so sort by id. A Set of applied ids gives a fast "already ran?" check. When everything ran, there is nothing to do.

questions.q: Finish checkTask so it applies the same rules as the lesson's constraints: the title (after trimming) must be 1 to 100 characters, and the priority a whole number from 1 to 3. Return an array of the names of the broken rules: "title", "priority", or both.
questions.explain: Checking in the API lets you answer with a clear 400 listing every problem. The database constraints stay in place as the last line of defence.

questions.q: Finish runAll(state, steps) so it behaves like a transaction. Each step is a function that changes the object it gets, and may throw. Work on a copy (structuredClone). If every step succeeds, return the copy. If any step throws, return the original state unchanged.
questions.explain: Changes go to a copy and are kept only if every step succeeds: that is atomicity. In the second call move ran, but its change was thrown away with the copy, just like a rollback.

questions.q: An index lets you find rows without reading them all. Finish buildIndex(rows, column): return a Map from each value of column to the array of ids of the rows with that value.
questions.explain: Building the map reads every row once; after that each lookup jumps straight to the answer. That is also why an index costs something on every write: it has to be kept up to date.
